01 / Introduction

Introduction and mathematical scope

A yield curve describes how the value of a future unit of money depends on its payment date. Constructing that curve is an inverse valuation problem: infer discount factors from a finite collection of instruments, then supply a defensible rule between and beyond their maturities.

In the option-pricing projects, discount factors and financing rates were inputs. Here they become the objects to estimate. A single constant rate can be useful for a first derivation, but a coupon bond, an interest-rate swap and a long-dated option all expose why different payment dates need different discounts. The central object is a function, rather than one number called “the interest rate”.

Three tasks should remain distinct. Construction translates instrument prices and contractual conventions into a curve. Calibration estimates parameters under a chosen loss function and constraints. Dynamics specifies how the curve evolves and under which probability measure. A smooth fit to today's observations completes neither a forecasting model nor an arbitrage-free dynamic pricing model.

An analogy: exchange rates between today and payment dates

A discount factor is the exchange rate between one unit paid at a future date and money today. Each payment date has its own exchange rate. A zero rate is a convenient annualized label for that exchange rate; a forward rate describes the exchange between two future dates. Changing the label's compounding convention should never change the underlying value.

Organization and prerequisites

Part I develops discount factors, rate conventions, instruments and bootstrapping. Part II studies interpolation, economic consistency, Nelson–Siegel and Svensson parameterizations, fitting and identification. Part III connects the curve to bond risk, scenarios and dynamic models, then supplies a laboratory, reproducible examples, a mathematical appendix and solved exercises.

The working framework uses a valuation date at time zero, positive discount factors and deterministic contractual cash flows. Curve rates may be negative. Default, collateral, liquidity and indexation are discussed explicitly; a government curve is not silently substituted for a collateral discount curve. The laboratory uses a simplified single-curve setting to make the mathematics transparent.

Conventions for every numerical example

Rates are annualized decimals internally: 3.5% means 0.035. One basis point is 0.0001, and one percentage point is 0.01. Time is measured in exact year fractions. Unless stated otherwise, zero and instantaneous forward rates use continuous compounding. A bond YTM or par coupon rate retains its stated payment frequency. Price amounts are per face value 100 unless a different face value is selected.

All fitted quotes, bond valuations, factor paths and scenarios on this page are synthetic. They were generated for this study and are not live market observations. The reference Svensson parameters are level 3.5%, slope −2%, first curvature 2.5%, second curvature −1.5%, and decay times 1.6 and 6.5 years. Static figures embed their numerical observations; the interactive laboratory computes its own curves offline.

Elementary calculus, present-value arithmetic and linear algebra are sufficient for the construction chapters. The dynamic-model discussion assumes some familiarity with stochastic processes and makes its probability-measure assumptions explicit. For readers arriving from Implied Volatility Surface, the same discipline applies: units, conventions and economic constraints are part of the model, rather than metadata added after calibration.

02 / Valuation coordinates

Discount factors and present-value representation

Let D(T)D(T) denote the time-zero price of a claim paying one unit at time TT, within a specified currency and discounting framework. Normalize D(0)=1D(0)=1. For deterministic payments CiC_i at dates tit_i, linear valuation gives:

P=∑i=1nCiD(ti),D(0)=1,D(T)>0.P=\sum_{i=1}^{n} C_iD(t_i),\qquad D(0)=1,\qquad D(T)>0.
(01)

This representation separates the instrument from the curve. The contract determines payment amounts and dates; the discounting model determines their present values. A fixed coupon bond contains a series of coupon claims and a principal claim. A zero-coupon bond contains only the terminal principal. The sum of present values is a dirty price, before any clean-price quotation adjustment.

What a discount factor contains

The relevant discount factor depends on the claim. A default-free unit in one currency, a collateralized derivative payment and an unsecured bank liability need not have the same present value. Differences in default exposure, collateral remuneration, funding and liquidity prevent their quotations from being pooled without a model of those differences.

For a deterministic short-rate path r(u)r(u), the value of a future unit is obtained by continuously discounting along the path. In a stochastic short-rate model under a suitable risk-neutral measure ℚ\mathbb Q, the default-free zero price is an expectation:

D(T)=exp(−∫0Tr(u)du)if rates are deterministic,D(T)=𝔼ℚ[exp(−∫0Trudu)]in a short-rate model.D(T)=\exp\left(-\int_0^T r(u)\,du\right) \quad\text{if rates are deterministic},\qquad D(T)=\mathbb E^{\mathbb Q}\left[\exp\left(-\int_0^T r_u\,du\right)\right] \quad\text{in a short-rate model}.
(02)

The stochastic expectation cannot generally be replaced by discounting at the expected short rate. The exponential is nonlinear. Jensen's inequality already explains why the distribution of accumulated rates matters, even before discussing correlations or risk premia.

Positive discounts and negative rates

Positive discount factors are essential to the usual logarithmic rate coordinates. They do not automatically imply D(T)≤1D(T)\le1 or that D(T)D(T) decreases with maturity. A negative-rate curve can price one future unit above one present unit. Whether this is compatible with an economic model depends on feasible funding and cash-storage alternatives. An assumption of freely accessible, costless zero-yield cash storage is stronger than the mathematical condition of positive discounts.

When all instantaneous forwards are nonnegative, discounts are decreasing. That implication is useful when the intended model prohibits negative rates, but it should not be imposed as a universal definition of arbitrage freedom. Later examples deliberately allow negative short-end rates.

A useful valuation check

In a flat 3% continuous curve, a payment of 100 in five years is worth 100e−0.03×5=86.0708100e^{-0.03\times5}=86.0708. Two payments of 50 at years two and five are worth 50e−0.06+50e−0.15=90.123650e^{-0.06}+50e^{-0.15}=90.1236. Moving part of the payment earlier increases value when the relevant discounts decrease. Under a sufficiently negative curve, the ordering can reverse; the mechanism is still the same present-value sum.

A production implementation should make this payment ledger visible. It catches missing principal, incorrect coupon frequency, duplicate payments and settlement-date mistakes before those errors are mistaken for unusual fitted rates. The laboratory below provides such a ledger for its selected bond.

03 / Rate conventions

Zero-coupon rates and compounding conventions

A zero rate annualizes the return between today and one payment date. Different compounding conventions give different numerical rates for the same discount factor. The continuously compounded zero rate z(T)z(T), a nominal rate ym(T)y_m(T) compounded mm times per year, and a simple rate L(T)L(T) satisfy:

D(T)=e−Tz(T)=(1+ym(T)m)−mT=11+TL(T).D(T)=e^{-Tz(T)}=\left(1+\frac{y_m(T)}m\right)^{-mT} =\frac{1}{1+TL(T)}.
(03)
z(T)=−lnD(T)T,ym(T)=m(ez(T)/m−1),L(T)=eTz(T)−1T.z(T)=-\frac{\ln D(T)}T,\qquad y_m(T)=m\left(e^{z(T)/m}-1\right),\qquad L(T)=\frac{e^{Tz(T)}-1}{T}.
(04)

The periodic formula requires 1+ym/m>01+y_m/m>0, while the simple formula requires 1+TL>01+TL>0. Continuous rates can be any finite real value because their discounts remain positive. These are domains of quotation formulas; an economic model can impose further restrictions.

Equivalent rates are not interchangeable inputs

A continuous rate of 4% is equivalent to a nominal semiannual rate of approximately 4.0403% and an effective annual rate of approximately 4.0811%. Discounting a five-year payment with 4% nominal semiannual compounding instead of 4% continuous compounding changes its present value. The numerical similarity of the rates does not justify mixing their formulas.

z=mln(1+ymm),yeff=ez−1,z=ln(1+yeff).z=m\ln\left(1+\frac{y_m}{m}\right),\qquad y_{\mathrm{eff}}=e^z-1,\qquad z=\ln(1+y_{\mathrm{eff}}).
(05)

The simple rate depends on the interval length. A simple one-year rate equivalent to 4% continuous is about 4.0811%, but the equivalent simple five-year annualized rate is about 4.4281%. “Simple annualized” does not mean one maturity-independent simple rate reproduces a flat continuous curve.

The short-maturity limit

The expression −lnD(T)/T-\ln D(T)/T is undefined at exactly zero. If the discount curve is differentiable there, use its limit. The instantaneous short-rate coordinate is −D'(0)-D'(0) because D(0)=1D(0)=1. Parametric models should implement this limit directly rather than evaluate a quotient of two small quantities.

z(0)=limT↓0−lnD(T)T=f(0)when the limit exists.z(0)=\lim_{T\downarrow0}-\frac{\ln D(T)}T=f(0) \quad\text{when the limit exists}.
(06)

Rates should carry four pieces of identifying information: currency, curve family, compounding convention and maturity or accrual period. A database column labelled “5Y yield” is incomplete if it does not distinguish a zero yield, a par swap rate, a coupon-bond YTM or a credit-spread-adjusted yield.

Numerical precision and reporting

Keep rates as decimals until display. A fitted residual of 0.000025 is 0.25 basis points, rather than 0.0025 basis points or 0.25 percentage points. Round the reporting layer, not the discount inputs. Rounding each zero rate before repricing can produce a meaningful price error on a large or long-duration portfolio.

The Bank of England explicitly identifies its published spot and forward curves as continuously compounded annual rates. That is a useful example of why a source's convention must be recorded before comparing it with another dataset. Bank of England yield-curve methodology.

Convention conversion is invertible within its domain. A practical test converts a discount to a quoted rate and back, then checks that the original discount is recovered to numerical precision. This checks both the rate formula and its unit handling without relying on a market price comparison.

04 / Forward representation

Forward rates and the integrated term structure

A forward rate describes an interval between future dates. In a deterministic single-curve framework, the discount ratio defines the time-zero forward value of a unit delivered over that interval. For 0≤t1<t20\le t_1<t_2, the continuously compounded interval forward is:

Fcc(t1,t2)=lnD(t1)−lnD(t2)t2−t1=t2z(t2)−t1z(t1)t2−t1.F_{\mathrm{cc}}(t_1,t_2)=\frac{\ln D(t_1)-\ln D(t_2)}{t_2-t_1} =\frac{t_2z(t_2)-t_1z(t_1)}{t_2-t_1}.
(07)

The corresponding simple forward uses the contract's accrual fraction α\alpha. The curve times and accrual fraction need not be numerically identical when their day-count conventions differ:

L(t1,t2)=D(t1)/D(t2)−1α.L(t_1,t_2)=\frac{D(t_1)/D(t_2)-1}{\alpha}.
(08)

For example, if D(1)=0.98D(1)=0.98, D(2)=0.95D(2)=0.95 and α=1\alpha=1, the simple forward is 3.1579%, while the continuous forward is approximately 3.1091%. Both reproduce the same discount ratio. They are different coordinates for the same interval value.

Instantaneous forwards

Taking the interval length to zero gives the instantaneous forward f(T)f(T). It is the local slope of accumulated discounting, rather than the slope of the zero-rate curve alone:

f(T)=−ddTlnD(T)=ddT[Tz(T)]=z(T)+Tz'(T).f(T)=-\frac{d}{dT}\ln D(T)=\frac{d}{dT}\left[Tz(T)\right] =z(T)+Tz'(T).
(09)
D(T)=exp(−∫0Tf(u)du),z(T)=1T∫0Tf(u)du.D(T)=\exp\left(-\int_0^T f(u)\,du\right),\qquad z(T)=\frac1T\int_0^T f(u)\,du.
(10)

These identities explain the geometry. A zero rate is an average of forwards from zero to maturity. If the zero curve rises at a given maturity, its marginal forward exceeds its average there. If it falls, its marginal forward is below the average. A flat zero curve has an equal constant forward curve.

An analogy: average speed and current speed

The zero rate resembles average speed over a journey from today to maturity. The instantaneous forward resembles speed at the journey's current endpoint. A higher current speed pulls the average upward, but the two need not coincide. Differentiating noisy average measurements can produce an even noisier estimate of current speed.

Forwards are not unconditional forecasts

A market-implied forward incorporates pricing, risk premia and the curve's construction assumptions. In a stochastic model, the expectation interpretation depends on the payoff, numeraire and probability measure. A simple forward associated with a traded rate can be a martingale under its appropriate forward measure; this does not make it the physical expected future policy rate.

Forwards extracted from a sovereign curve can also contain liquidity and credit effects. Interpreting an observed hump as an expected sequence of central-bank decisions requires assumptions that the discount-ratio calculation itself does not supply. The arithmetic is precise; its macroeconomic interpretation is conditional.

Internal consistency checks

For a differentiable parametric curve, compute forwards analytically and compare them with a numerical derivative of Tz(T)Tz(T). Then integrate the forward back to the zero rate. A disagreement identifies an implementation error or an inconsistent interpolation choice. At an interpolation knot with a derivative jump, compare the appropriate one-sided derivatives rather than demand a unique value that the model has not defined.

05 / Coupon instruments

Par yields and yields to maturity

Three rates can coexist at the same maturity: the zero rate of a single payment, the coupon rate that makes a bond worth par, and the yield to maturity of a particular coupon bond. Their differences are structural, even when all instruments use one curve.

The par coupon rate

For face value NN, a regular bond with mm coupons per year, maturity T=n/mT=n/m, annual coupon rate cc, and no accrued interest has price NN when:

1=cpar(T)m∑j=1nD(j/m)+D(T),cpar(T)=m[1−D(T)]∑j=1nD(j/m).1=\frac{c_{\mathrm{par}}(T)}m\sum_{j=1}^{n}D(j/m)+D(T),\qquad c_{\mathrm{par}}(T)=\frac{m[1-D(T)]}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}D(j/m)}.
(11)

For an irregular coupon schedule with accrual fractions αj\alpha_j, replace the denominator by ∑jαjD(tj)\sum_j\alpha_jD(t_j). The terminal principal remains separate. The par rate therefore uses all coupon-date discounts, not just the terminal discount. On a nonflat curve it generally differs from the terminal zero rate, even after aligning compounding conventions.

A par swap rate has a related annuity denominator, but the floating-leg numerator depends on the forecasting and discounting curves. The expression 1−D(T)1-D(T) is the familiar single-curve, spot-starting case. It should not be carried into a multicurve valuation unchanged.

The bond's single internal rate

For a regular bond priced on a coupon date, nominal YTM yy, compounded at the coupon frequency, solves:

P=∑j=1nNc/m(1+y/m)j+N(1+y/m)n,y>−m.P=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{Nc/m}{(1+y/m)^j} +\frac{N}{(1+y/m)^n},\qquad y>-m.
(12)

With nonnegative coupons and positive principal, price is strictly decreasing in yy, so a positive observed price has a unique root in the admissible domain. A bracketing root solver is preferable to unconstrained Newton steps near the lower boundary. At irregular settlement dates, exponents and conventions must match the bond's actual quotation rules.

YTM compresses multiple curve discounts into one internal rate. Two bonds with identical maturity but different coupon amounts usually have different YTMs when the curve is nonflat. This does not establish an arbitrage between them: their payment timing differs. A high-coupon bond puts more weight on early-date discounts.

Yield is not a guaranteed holding-period return

A bond's YTM becomes the realized compound return through maturity only under suitable assumptions about payment, purchase price and coupon reinvestment at that yield. Selling before maturity adds exposure to the future curve and any change in credit or liquidity. Even a default-free bond can generate a holding-period return different from its initial YTM.

The reference five-year bond pays a 4% annual coupon semiannually. Its curve price is 103.660106 and its nominal semiannual YTM is 3.201986%. Its terminal continuous zero rate is 3.191752%. The coupon, terminal zero and YTM each answer a different question. The small numerical difference between the latter two is specific to this example.

When graphing par and zero rates together, identify whether conventions have been aligned. This page converts its semiannual par coupon to a continuous equivalent 2ln(1+cpar/2)2\ln(1+c_{\mathrm{par}}/2) in comparison plots, while explicitly retaining nominal conventions in YTM tables. Conversion aligns the rate scale; it does not turn a coupon-weighted rate into a zero rate.

06 / Contract specification

Schedules, day counts and quotation conventions

The discount function is only one part of a price. A schedule generator determines accrual start dates, accrual end dates, reset dates, fixing dates and payment dates. These can differ. A model that uses the right rates at the wrong dates is still a wrong valuation model.

Curve time and coupon accrual

A curve may measure time using Actual/365 Fixed while an instrument uses a different convention for its coupon accrual. Keep these quantities separate. If tjt_j is the curve year fraction to payment and αj\alpha_j the instrument's accrual fraction, a fixed coupon cash flow is NcαjNc\alpha_j and its present value is NcαjD(tj)Nc\alpha_jD(t_j).

αAct/365F=actual days365,αAct/360=actual days360,Cj=Ncαj.\alpha_{\mathrm{Act/365F}}=\frac{\text{actual days}}{365},\qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{Act/360}}=\frac{\text{actual days}}{360},\qquad C_j=Nc\alpha_j.
(13)

For an interval of exactly 181 days, these fractions are approximately 0.495890 and 0.502778. At an annual coupon of 4% on face 100, the associated interest amounts are 1.983562 and 2.011111. A convention change is a change in contractual accrual, not simply a display preference.

Actual/Actual is a family of conventions, and 30/360 also has several variants. Leap years, coupon-period denominators, month-end rules and treatment of February must follow the selected contract convention. A generic “days divided by 365” implementation should not be advertised as supporting all bonds.

Clean price, dirty price and accrued interest

The discounted value of remaining cash flows is the dirty price paid at settlement, subject to the instrument's settlement rules. The clean quoted price excludes accrued interest:

Pdirty=Pclean+AI,AI=Cnextaccrual elapsedfull accrual periodunder proportional-period accrual.P_{\mathrm{dirty}}=P_{\mathrm{clean}}+AI,\qquad AI=C_{\mathrm{next}}\frac{\text{accrual elapsed}}{\text{full accrual period}} \quad\text{under proportional-period accrual}.
(14)

For a regular semiannual 4% coupon on face 100, the full coupon is 2. If 40% of the coupon accrual period has elapsed, accrued interest is 0.8. A clean quote of 101.2 then corresponds to a dirty amount of 102.0. This simplified proportional rule needs modification for contracts with ex-coupon treatment or other conventions.

Calendar adjustments and settlement

A business-day adjustment moves a date according to a calendar and a convention such as following, modified following or preceding. The adjusted payment date need not replace the accrual end date. A payment lag introduces another distinction. Apply calendars to their intended fields and avoid deriving all dates from a single adjusted timestamp.

Settlement after the valuation date may require forward discounting from the valuation date to settlement, cash-flow eligibility checks and an accrued-interest calculation as of settlement. Stubs, amortization, floating-rate fixings and redemption premiums alter the payment ledger. A bond purchased just before a coupon date should not accidentally receive a coupon to which the buyer is not entitled.

Scope of the numerical laboratory

The laboratory deliberately values regular fixed-rate bonds on a coupon date, with exact-year intervals and zero accrued interest. It requires maturity multiplied by coupon frequency to be an integer. It supports annual, semiannual and quarterly payments but does not generate real calendars, stubs or ex-coupon periods. This makes the arithmetic reproducible while identifying exactly which contract layer a market implementation would add.

Validate schedules before optimizing curve parameters. Compare payment counts, total principal and coupon amounts against an independent contract description. Otherwise a calibration can absorb schedule errors into strange curvature coefficients, producing a small residual with an incorrect economic interpretation.

07 / Market inputs

Market instruments and curve families

A curve is identified by both its purpose and its inputs. Government securities, overnight-index swaps, deposits, futures and tenor swaps contain different contractual and risk information. Selecting instruments is part of model specification.

Government bond curves

A sovereign curve can be fitted directly to coupon-bond prices after generating each bond's cash flows. On-the-run securities may carry liquidity premia; bills and bonds can have different market microstructure; securities with special repo demand can be unusually expensive. Pooling every bond into an equal-weight fit can turn these instrument effects into artificial term-structure features.

Use an eligibility policy for embedded options, unusual redemption provisions, stale quotes and securities with distinctive liquidity treatment. A bond with a call option is not a deterministic cash-flow observation unless its option value is modelled separately. Inflation-linked securities require an indexation framework and cannot be treated as nominal fixed coupons.

Deposits, forwards and futures

A deposit supplies a short-period simple-rate relation. A forward rate agreement supplies a rate for a future accrual period, subject to its settlement convention. A futures quote can be converted into an implied futures rate, but the corresponding forward rate can differ because of daily settlement and correlation with funding rates. A futures-forward convexity adjustment belongs to a dynamic model, rather than a static identity that can be guessed from one quote.

Near-term fixings and known overnight accruals may anchor portions of the short end. Quotes spanning a policy meeting can contain concentrated timing information that a smooth global function will average away. Whether that is acceptable depends on whether the curve is intended for broad economic analysis or precise short-dated instrument pricing.

Overnight and tenor-dependent curves

Under idealized daily collateralization remunerated at an overnight benchmark, discounting is associated with the collateral rate. An OIS curve therefore has a different role from an unsecured term-rate forecasting curve. The precise collateral agreement, currency, payment lag and settlement conventions matter. Uncollateralized trades or cross-currency collateral introduce further adjustments.

A tenor-specific forecasting curve can represent projected fixings for one reference index, while a common collateral curve discounts their payments. Basis-swap quotes help connect different tenor forecasts. The word “curve” should therefore include identifiers for currency, collateral framework and reference tenor.

Data selection and measurement uncertainty

Bid and ask are an uncertainty interval, not two independent exact equilibrium prices. Synchronized quotes, source quality, trade timestamps and liquidity should be recorded. A thinly traded long-end bond does not deserve unlimited influence merely because its maturity is unique. Nor should an illiquid observation be excluded simply because it disagrees with a preferred smooth shape; the exclusion needs a reproducible reason.

The ECB describes zero, forward and par curves derived from selected euro-area government bonds and uses a Svensson representation. This illustrates a curve with a defined universe and methodology, rather than one generic curve for every euro claim. ECB yield-curve methodology. The Federal Reserve's Treasury-curve research similarly emphasizes instrument selection and smooth estimation. Gürkaynak, Sack and Wright.

The laboratory uses synthetic zero-rate observations directly. Real government-bond calibration would instead start from bond quotations and a cash-flow engine. Treating those synthetic zeros as already available isolates parameter estimation; it does not reproduce the full market-data construction pipeline.

08 / Sequential construction

Bootstrapping deposits and zero-coupon claims

Bootstrapping solves for discount factors in a sequence of maturities, using previously identified values where possible. The simplest instruments expose individual nodes directly.

A deposit node

For a spot-starting deposit with simple rate LL, year fraction α\alpha, one unit lent today and repayment 1+αL1+\alpha L, the single-curve discount is:

1=(1+αL)D(T),D(T)=11+αL.1=(1+\alpha L)D(T),\qquad D(T)=\frac{1}{1+\alpha L}.
(15)

At a 3% simple rate for an exact half-year interval, D(0.5)=1/1.015=0.985222D(0.5)=1/1.015=0.985222. The associated continuous zero rate is ln(1.015)/0.5=2.977722%\ln(1.015)/0.5=2.977722\%. The rate conversion and bootstrap are consistent because they reproduce the same repayment value.

If the deposit begins at a future settlement date tst_s, the relation uses the ratio D(T)/D(ts)D(T)/D(t_s), rather than automatically setting the starting discount to one. Settlement lags require a starting node or an explicit short-end assumption. In a credit-sensitive deposit market, the relation belongs to the deposit's curve framework, not automatically the collateral curve.

A zero-coupon price node

A zero-coupon claim with face value NN and price PP directly identifies D(T)=P/ND(T)=P/N, when both cash flows belong to the intended curve. A price of 95 per 100 payable in two years identifies D(2)=0.95D(2)=0.95 and a continuous zero of about 2.564665%. No coupon interpolation is needed at that instrument's maturity.

A known forward period

When a simple forward L(t1,t2)L(t_1,t_2) and starting discount are known, the ending node follows recursively:

D(t2)=D(t1)1+αL(t1,t2).D(t_2)=\frac{D(t_1)}{1+\alpha L(t_1,t_2)}.
(16)

The denominator must be positive. Negative simple forwards are allowed if the denominator remains positive; they produce an ending discount larger than the starting discount. A failure of the positivity domain signals inconsistent inputs or a quotation error before any optimizer is involved.

Information versus assumptions

A finite collection of zero prices supplies a finite collection of discounts. It does not uniquely determine every intermediate discount. Bootstrapping alone is not a complete continuous curve model; interpolation fills the gaps. Instruments with payment dates inside those gaps can force interpolation into the bootstrap itself.

An analogy: solving a triangular system

If the first equation contains only the first unknown, solve it. If the second contains that known value and one new unknown, solve the second. Continue down the system. This is the ideal bootstrap. Once an equation involves several still-unknown intermediate dates, a rule connecting those dates is needed before the triangular logic can continue.

After obtaining each node, reprice the instrument that generated it. This distinguishes an algebraic error from the later modelling decision used between nodes. Record the original quote, convention, solved node and pricing residual together. A discount table without those inputs cannot be reliably audited.

09 / Cash-flow equations

Bootstrapping coupon bonds and par swaps

Coupon instruments combine several dates in one observed price. If all earlier coupon-date discounts are already known, isolate the final discount algebraically. For a regular bond with coupon amount CC each period:

P=C∑j=1n−1D(tj)+(N+C)D(T),D(T)=P−C∑j=1n−1D(tj)N+C.P=C\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}D(t_j)+(N+C)D(T),\qquad D(T)=\frac{P-C\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}D(t_j)}{N+C}.
(17)

Use dirty price PP. A clean quotation that omits accrued interest cannot be placed into this equation unchanged. For amortizing principal or irregular coupons, replace the simplified final cash flow and coupon amounts with the actual ledger.

Annual par instruments

A synthetic annual par bond or idealized single-curve par swap with maturity nn and annual rate SnS_n satisfies 1=Sn∑j=1nD(j)+D(n)1=S_n\sum_{j=1}^{n}D(j)+D(n). The recursion is:

D(n)=1−Sn∑j=1n−1D(j)1+Sn.D(n)=\frac{1-S_n\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}D(j)}{1+S_n}.
(18)

Generate three such quotations from continuous zero rates 2%, 2.5% and 3% at years one, two and three. The resulting annual par rates are approximately 2.020134%, 2.525104% and 3.024884%. Applying the recursion recovers the original discounts. These are distinct annual coupon and continuous zero conventions.

33.024884%0.9139311853.000000%

The floating-leg telescoping argument

In an idealized single-curve swap, a floating coupon projected over (tj−1,tj)(t_{j-1},t_j) has discounted value αjLjD(tj)=D(tj−1)−D(tj)\alpha_jL_jD(t_j)=D(t_{j-1})-D(t_j). Summing coupons telescopes to D(t0)−D(T)D(t_0)-D(T). For a spot-starting swap with t0=0t_0=0, this is 1−D(T)1-D(T). The par fixed rate is the floating-leg present value divided by the fixed-leg annuity.

S=D(t0)−D(T)∑j=1nαjD(tj)under matched single-curve conventions.S=\frac{D(t_0)-D(T)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_jD(t_j)} \quad\text{under matched single-curve conventions}.
(19)

The assumptions matter: one curve forecasts and discounts, payment dates align with the derivation, and coupons have not already fixed differently. OIS compounded accruals, payment lags, known fixings and multicurve forecasts can require a fuller cash-flow treatment.

Missing intermediate nodes

Suppose the available swaps mature at two and five years, but the five-year fixed leg pays annually. Discounts at years three and four are not yet observed. Solving the five-year equation therefore needs an interpolation rule involving the proposed five-year endpoint. A root solver can determine that endpoint while regenerating the intermediate discounts on every candidate.

With a global spline, changing a distant endpoint can change earlier interpolated values, so a simple one-pass bootstrap may not remain exact. Iteration or a joint solve is then appropriate. Interpolation and construction must be designed together; they are not always separable postprocessing steps. Hagan and West, Interpolation Methods for Curve Construction.

Exact fitting and noisy markets

An exact bootstrap reproduces selected input quotes by construction, but it may transmit stale data or bid–ask noise directly into forwards. A smooth parametric fit sacrifices exact repricing to reduce local noise and estimate a coherent broad shape. The choice depends on the task: instrument valuation, hedging, economic interpretation and forecasting can prioritize different properties.

Always inspect both the fitted object and instrument residuals. Smooth-looking zero rates can conceal implausible forwards; tiny price residuals can coexist with unstable node sensitivities. Neither visual smoothness nor exact input repricing is a complete quality criterion.

10 / Curve architecture

Discounting, forecasting and multicurve valuation

A modern curve architecture can use one function for collateral discounting and another for projecting a tenor-specific floating index. Denote the discount curve by DcD^c and the projected simple fixing for period jj by LjxL_j^x. A swap's par fixed rate is determined by:

S=∑j=1nαjLjxDc(pj)∑k=1mδkDc(qk).S=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_j L_j^xD^c(p_j)} {\sum_{k=1}^{m}\delta_kD^c(q_k)}.
(20)

Here pjp_j and qkq_k are the actual floating and fixed payment dates, and αj,δk\alpha_j,\delta_k their respective accrual fractions. The notional cancels for a constant-notional par swap. Known fixings replace projected values where applicable.

Why the numerator need not telescope

If LjxL_j^x is generated from a different forecasting curve, multiplying by Dc(pj)D^c(p_j) does not produce a difference of discount-curve nodes. The single-curve numerator 1−D(T)1-D(T) is therefore not a general multicurve identity. Distinguishing the two roles is essential when reproducing swap quotes.

A forecasting curve may be represented by positive auxiliary quantities Qx(t)Q^x(t), with Ljx=[Qx(tj−1)/Qx(tj)−1]/αjL_j^x=[Q^x(t_{j-1})/Q^x(t_j)-1]/\alpha_j. These quantities are often called pseudo-discounts. They parameterize projected rates but are not necessarily traded zero-coupon prices. An arbitrage argument applying to genuine discount factors cannot automatically be applied to them.

Calibration order and basis information

A common construction sequence first anchors a collateral discount curve with suitable overnight instruments, then fits a tenor forecast curve using deposits, forwards and swaps referencing that tenor, and finally uses basis instruments to connect additional tenors. Some sets of instruments require a joint iterative solve because curves enter one another's valuation equations.

A basis spread can compensate for differences between projected floating legs. It is not generally a single constant added to all zero rates. The valuation weights, payment frequencies and accrual conventions affect how quoted basis information maps to node values. One should calibrate the instrument equation that defines the quote.

Collateral assumptions

The simple overnight-discounting rule assumes an appropriate collateral agreement with frequent margining and remuneration at the benchmark being modelled. Thresholds, optional collateral currencies, funding costs and counterparty exposure can make the actual valuation more complex. State the framework instead of calling every selected curve universally risk free.

Bianchetti's multiple-curve research explains the separation between forwarding and discounting and the resulting role of basis information. The algebra in this section is the elementary deterministic version of that architecture. Two Curves, One Price.

Risk implications

A bump to a discount quote and a bump to a forecasting quote need not move the same cash-flow components. Hedge reports should identify which curve was recalibrated, what quotes were bumped and whether other curves were held fixed or rebuilt. A single portfolio DV01 can hide substantial offsetting discount and forecast exposures.

This page's laboratory uses one curve for deterministic fixed-bond cash flows. It demonstrates zero, forward and par transformations within that setting. It does not claim to bootstrap a full OIS/tenor system or price a collateralized swap from market data. The separation developed here is the architectural extension needed for that application.

11 / Continuous construction

Interpolation of discounts, zeros and forwards

Observed nodes do not determine a unique continuous curve. Choosing the quantity to interpolate changes intermediate discounts, forwards and hedges, even when every node is fitted exactly. It is often useful to work with integrated rates h(T)=−lnD(T)=Tz(T)h(T)=-\ln D(T)=Tz(T), because discount positivity then follows automatically.

Log-linear discount interpolation

Between nodes tit_i and ti+1t_{i+1}, set w=(T−ti)/(ti+1−ti)w=(T-t_i)/(t_{i+1}-t_i). Linear interpolation of the log discount is:

lnD(T)=(1−w)lnD(ti)+wlnD(ti+1),f(T)=−lnD(ti+1)−lnD(ti)ti+1−ti.\ln D(T)=(1-w)\ln D(t_i)+w\ln D(t_{i+1}),\qquad f(T)=-\frac{\ln D(t_{i+1})-\ln D(t_i)}{t_{i+1}-t_i}.
(21)

Discount factors remain positive and the instantaneous forward is constant within each interval. Forwards typically jump at knots. The zero curve is continuous away from the origin, but its derivative can jump. This is a simple, local and interpretable construction; it is not a smooth-forward construction.

Linear zero-rate interpolation

If z(T)=zi+si(T−ti)z(T)=z_i+s_i(T-t_i), then f(T)=z(T)+Tsif(T)=z(T)+Ts_i. The forward is linear inside the interval and can jump at the next knot when the zero slope changes. A straight zero segment therefore does not imply a constant forward segment. Including a zero-time limit requires a deliberate short-end node or boundary rule.

Linear discount interpolation

Directly interpolating positive discount nodes produces positive discounts between them. If D(T)=Di+si(T−ti)D(T)=D_i+s_i(T-t_i), its instantaneous forward is −si/D(T)-s_i/D(T). That is generally curved inside each interval. Extrapolating the same linear formula indefinitely can cross zero, even when interpolation inside the observed interval is safe.

Locality and numerical derivatives

Local interpolation uses nearby nodes, which often makes sensitivities easier to interpret. A change to one node affects neighboring intervals rather than the whole curve. Global interpolants can create distant changes when one input is bumped. The smoother result may be desirable, but the resulting risk footprint should be understood.

At a discontinuous forward knot there is no unique two-sided derivative of lnD\ln D. A software implementation can choose a left or right convention for reporting, while valuation uses the continuous discount itself. A finite difference that straddles the knot averages two sides and should not be presented as the model's unique instantaneous forward.

Interpolation and repricing

If an input instrument pays between nodes, its price depends on the interpolation choice. Replacing an interpolator after calibration can therefore destroy exact repricing. Rebuild or recalibrate under the new interpolation rule and record the change in residuals and sensitivities.

Hagan and West analyze the joint problem of interpolation and construction and discuss methods designed around forward-rate behavior. Their work is useful precisely because a visually smooth zero curve is not enough to characterize a satisfactory pricing curve. Interpolation Methods for Curve Construction.

12 / Nonparametric estimation

Splines, smoothing and regularization

A spline joins low-degree polynomial segments while enforcing selected continuity conditions at knots. It supplies more flexibility than a small parametric family, but that flexibility must be controlled. A curve can interpolate every noisy quote and still produce unstable forwards.

The interpolated coordinate matters

A cubic spline on zero rates is different from a cubic spline on discounts or integrated rates. Splining h(T)=Tz(T)h(T)=Tz(T) makes f(T)=h'(T)f(T)=h'(T) directly available and guarantees positive discounts through D=e−hD=e^{-h}. It does not by itself guarantee positive forwards, monotonicity or a sensible extrapolation.

A natural cubic spline imposes zero second derivatives at its boundary knots. That is a mathematical boundary condition, rather than a universal economic fact about the curve's short or long end. A shape-preserving piecewise cubic method such as PCHIP can preserve monotonicity of the interpolated coordinate when its node data are monotone, but generally sacrifices continuity of higher derivatives.

Fitting rather than exact interpolation

A smoothing formulation combines a data loss with a roughness penalty. For observed zero rates yiy_i, one illustrative objective is:

minh{∑iwi[h(Ti)Ti−yi]2+λ∫ab[h''(u)]2du},h(0)=0.\min_h\left\{\sum_i w_i\left[\frac{h(T_i)}{T_i}-y_i\right]^2 +\lambda\int_a^b [h''(u)]^2\,du\right\},\qquad h(0)=0.
(22)

The first term measures zero-rate fit; the second penalizes changes in the forward curve because h''=f'h''=f'. A different penalty, such as an integral of f''f'' squared, controls a different notion of smoothness. The penalty's units and normalization matter when comparing λ\lambda across datasets or maturity ranges.

At λ=0\lambda=0, a sufficiently flexible representation can track every observation. Larger λ\lambda suppresses local variation and increases residuals. Choose the trade-off using the intended pricing and risk task, quote uncertainty and validation, rather than the smoothest-looking chart alone.

Constraints and shape preservation

If the modelling framework requires nonnegative forwards, impose h'≥0h'\ge0 explicitly or use a construction that enforces it. If negative rates are economically admissible, an unconditional monotonicity constraint on hh can erase valid market structure. Bounds on forwards can be helpful numerical regularizers but should be named as modelling assumptions.

Exact interpolation through noisy observations can create forward oscillations because differentiation amplifies local errors. Increasing spline smoothness is not always enough: a highly smooth function can still oscillate between sparse points. Knot placement, penalties, constraints and the coordinate being fitted must be evaluated together.

Complexity and reproducibility

Record knot locations, degree, boundary conditions, objective weights and penalty settings with the fitted curve. A label such as “cubic spline” does not identify a reproducible model. Examine quote residuals, forward shape, bump sensitivities and extrapolation separately.

The figure uses a natural cubic spline and PCHIP on the same synthetic integrated-rate nodes. It illustrates derivative behavior, without claiming that either is a universal market standard or that the PCHIP example implements monotone convex interpolation. The parametric chapters next make a different trade-off: fewer degrees of freedom, clearer broad-shape interpretation, and less ability to reproduce local detail.

13 / Model constraints

Economic consistency and admissible rate curves

Consistency begins with correct valuation identities and a clearly stated economic framework. There is no single curve-shape checklist that replaces those assumptions. In particular, negative rates and increasing discounts must be treated differently from negative discount factors.

Basic coordinate requirements

For finite logarithmic rates, require positive discounts and D(0)=1D(0)=1. A differentiable discount curve determines a consistent instantaneous forward through −D'/D-D'/D. Integrating that forward must recover the same discount curve. Positive cash flows valued with positive discounts have positive present values.

D(T)=e−h(T),h(0)=0,f(T)=h'(T).D(T)=e^{-h(T)},\qquad h(0)=0,\qquad f(T)=h'(T).
(23)

This representation guarantees positive DD for every finite real hh. It does not constrain the sign of ff. Nonnegative forwards imply hh is nondecreasing and DD is nonincreasing; permitting negative forwards relaxes that condition.

The role of cash storage and funding

In an idealized world with costless, unlimited storage of zero-yield cash and unrestricted borrowing against future receipts, a default-free claim priced above its payoff can create a dominance argument. Actual negative-rate modelling allows frictions or institutional constraints that invalidate the costless-storage alternative. The appropriate admissibility restriction follows from that framework.

A smooth finite forward curve, including negative values, can serve as the deterministic rate path of a consistent deterministic-rate model when the funding assumptions permit it. Therefore negative forwards alone do not establish an implementation error. They should still trigger a check of quotation units, curve identity and intended rate regime.

Static fit versus dynamic no arbitrage

A fitted cross-section describes prices at one date. An arbitrary stochastic evolution of its parameters can generate inconsistent bond-price drifts, even if the curve remains positive and smooth at every date. Dynamic no-arbitrage conditions link drift and volatility under the pricing measure. They are additional restrictions on time evolution.

Conversely, a theoretically arbitrage-free dynamic model can fit observed bond prices poorly because the selected instruments contain liquidity, credit or convention effects outside the model. Economic consistency and empirical accuracy are related but distinct criteria.

Instrument-level checks

Reprice the actual calibration instruments, use matched clean/dirty conventions, and compare residuals with quotation resolution or bid–ask widths. Check that the predicted prices respond correctly to controlled shocks. A curve that yields a small zero-rate RMSE can still produce material long-bond price errors because duration amplifies yield differences.

In a multicurve architecture, pseudo-discounts should not be treated as freely tradable discount claims. Basis relationships must be checked through the relevant instrument equations. Arbitrage tests that combine unrelated sovereign, collateral and tenor curves as if they priced identical claims can diagnose an inconsistency that the market never asserted.

Useful diagnostics are explicit: positivity, endpoint normalization, repricing, forward-integral recovery, interpolation continuity and sensitivity stability. The conclusion should state what each check establishes. “No negative forwards” is a rate-regime test; “prices recover to tolerance” is a calibration test; neither alone proves a fully specified stochastic model has no arbitrage.

14 / Parametric representation

The Nelson–Siegel term-structure model

Nelson–Siegel represents broad curve shapes using three rate coefficients and one positive decay time. Its forward-rate form makes the interpretation especially clear. Let τ>0\tau>0 and x=T/τx=T/\tau:

fNS(T)=β0+β1e−x+β2xe−x.f_{\mathrm{NS}}(T)=\beta_0+\beta_1e^{-x}+\beta_2xe^{-x}.
(24)

The first loading is constant, the second decays from one to zero, and the third starts at zero, rises and then decays. Integrating from zero to TT gives the continuous zero-rate representation:

zNS(T)=β0+β1A(x)+β2B(x),A(x)=1−e−xx,B(x)=A(x)−e−x.z_{\mathrm{NS}}(T)=\beta_0+\beta_1A(x)+\beta_2B(x),\qquad A(x)=\frac{1-e^{-x}}x,\qquad B(x)=A(x)-e^{-x}.
(25)

The coefficients have rate units and the loadings are dimensionless. The decay time has units of years. Some publications use a decay speed λ=1/τ\lambda=1/\tau instead; increasing a speed compresses the maturity scale, while increasing a time stretches it. Mixing those conventions reverses the parameter's interpretation.

Endpoint limits

z(0)=f(0)=β0+β1,limT→∞z(T)=limT→∞f(T)=β0.z(0)=f(0)=\beta_0+\beta_1,\qquad \lim_{T\to\infty}z(T)=\lim_{T\to\infty}f(T)=\beta_0.
(26)

Thus β0\beta_0 controls the asymptotic level and β1\beta_1 controls the short-minus-long difference. A negative slope coefficient makes the short limit lower than the long limit. β2\beta_2 adds medium-horizon curvature without changing either endpoint limit.

Where curvature appears

The forward curvature loading xe−xxe^{-x} reaches its maximum at x=1x=1, or T=τT=\tau. The zero curvature loading B(x)B(x) reaches its maximum at approximately x=1.793x=1.793. The maximum of the complete fitted curve need not occur at either location because the slope loading also contributes. A decay parameter is therefore not generally the maturity of the curve's peak.

Holding other coefficients fixed, increasing β0\beta_0 shifts the entire zero curve by a constant. Increasing β1\beta_1 predominantly raises short maturities. Increasing β2\beta_2 raises the middle of the curve. Changing τ\tau alters both slope and curvature loadings, moving their maturity scale while preserving the endpoint limits.

Parsimony and limitations

The family can describe upward, downward and hump-shaped curves with few parameters. This makes it useful for broad economic summaries and factor modelling. It cannot reproduce every combination of local policy-date features, liquidity effects and multiple humps. A residual pattern can reflect limited model flexibility rather than a failed optimizer.

Conditional on τ\tau, the zero model is linear in the three coefficients. This separability is computationally valuable: estimate the coefficients by linear least squares inside a one-dimensional nonlinear search for decay. The original author research develops this parsimonious representation and its estimation. Nelson and Siegel, NBER working paper.

Stable evaluation near zero

Direct subtraction of 1−e−x1-e^{-x} loses precision for tiny xx. Use an exponential-minus-one function or a Taylor series. Define A(0)=1A(0)=1 and B(0)=0B(0)=0 explicitly. These limits preserve the short rate and prevent a spurious hole at the origin in plots, calibration and CSV exports.

15 / Parametric flexibility

The Svensson extension and a second curvature factor

Svensson adds a second curvature component at a separate positive decay time. Let x1=T/τ1x_1=T/\tau_1 and x2=T/τ2x_2=T/\tau_2. The continuous zero and instantaneous forward rates are:

zNSS(T)=β0+β1A(x1)+β2B(x1)+β3B(x2).z_{\mathrm{NSS}}(T)=\beta_0+\beta_1A(x_1)+\beta_2B(x_1)+\beta_3B(x_2).
(27)
fNSS(T)=β0+β1e−x1+β2x1e−x1+β3x2e−x2.f_{\mathrm{NSS}}(T)=\beta_0+\beta_1e^{-x_1} +\beta_2x_1e^{-x_1}+\beta_3x_2e^{-x_2}.
(28)

There are four rate coefficients and two decay times. The extra loading vanishes at both endpoints, so the short and long limits remain β0+β1\beta_0+\beta_1 and β0\beta_0. It allows an additional hump or dip across maturities. When β3=0\beta_3=0, the model reduces to Nelson–Siegel and τ2\tau_2 becomes unidentifiable from prices.

Additional flexibility has an identification cost

If τ1=τ2\tau_1=\tau_2, the two curvature columns are identical. Only their sum β2+β3\beta_2+\beta_3 is identified. When the decay times are merely close, the columns are nearly dependent; large opposite coefficients can produce a moderate fitted curve. A small residual can therefore coexist with unstable parameters.

Sparse long-end observations can make the long level and second curvature partially compensate for one another. Different combinations may price observed maturities almost equally well but imply different extrapolated rates. Report the curve and its out-of-sample consequences, rather than interpret each coefficient as a uniquely measured economic quantity.

Parameter domains and conventions

Positive decay times are essential to the standard decaying basis. Rate coefficients may have either sign. Additional coefficient bounds, decay bounds or ordering rules are numerical and modelling choices. Ordering τ1<τ2\tau_1<\tau_2 can simplify a particular implementation, but it restricts how the slope-associated first scale and the second curvature scale are assigned.

The browser fit imposes positive bounded decay times and coefficient magnitudes at most 15%. It does not impose an ordering between the two decay times. Rank-deficient candidates are rejected. These safeguards keep the educational search finite and reproducible; they do not establish that the selected solution is the unique global optimum.

Reference shape and sources

The reference curve combines a short-end rise with a modest long-middle dip. Its second curvature coefficient is negative. The extra term lowers medium-to-long rates without altering the limiting level. At 30 years the zero is still about 3.219731%, below its 3.5% asymptote because the curvature and slope contributions have not vanished completely.

Svensson introduced the extension for estimating and interpreting forward rates. Its use in institutional curve fitting makes it a natural companion to Nelson–Siegel, but institutional implementations differ in objectives, instrument selection and numerical details. Svensson, Estimating and Interpreting Forward Interest Rates. A cross-country methodological survey is available in BIS Papers No. 25.

Choosing Svensson because it fits better in-sample is only the beginning. Test residuals, withheld maturities, parameter stability and extrapolation. If the extra factor reduces training error but substantially increases uncertainty where risk is concentrated, the simpler model may remain more useful for the intended application.

16 / Statistical estimation

Calibration objectives and observation weights

A calibration is defined by its observations, residual coordinate, weights and admissible parameter set. “Best-fitting curve” is incomplete without those choices. Fitting bond prices, bond yields and extracted zero rates generally produces different parameter estimates.

Zero-rate least squares

When continuous zero-rate observations yiy_i are available at maturities TiT_i, a common loss is:

Jz(p)=∑i∈Iwi[z(Ti;p)−yi]2,wi>0.J_z(p)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}w_i[z(T_i;p)-y_i]^2,\qquad w_i>0.
(29)

Equal weights make one basis point at a short maturity as costly as one basis point at a long maturity. Weights proportional to inverse measurement variance can be appropriate if those variances are defensibly estimated. Dense clusters of similar maturities can otherwise dominate the fit simply because more observations are available there.

Price-space calibration

For coupon bonds with dirty price observations PiobsP_i^{\mathrm{obs}}, fit their full cash-flow sums:

Pi(p)=∑jCije−tijz(tij;p),JP(p)=∑iwi[Pi(p)−Piobs]2.P_i(p)=\sum_j C_{ij}e^{-t_{ij}z(t_{ij};p)},\qquad J_P(p)=\sum_i w_i[P_i(p)-P_i^{\mathrm{obs}}]^2.
(30)

Price fitting avoids treating an extracted zero curve as error-free raw data. It also preserves contract information. Equal price weights can give long-duration bonds more influence over rate fit because a given yield error creates a larger price residual there. Normalize by face value when instruments have different notionals.

Duration normalization

For a small approximately parallel yield discrepancy, ΔPi≈−PiDiΔyi\Delta P_i\approx-P_i\mathcal D_i\Delta y_i, where Di\mathcal D_i is duration under the chosen yield convention. Dividing a price residual by PiDiP_i\mathcal D_i approximately converts it to a yield residual:

Jscaled(p)=∑i[Pi(p)−PiobsPiobsDi]2.J_{\mathrm{scaled}}(p)=\sum_i \left[\frac{P_i(p)-P_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{P_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\mathcal D_i}\right]^2.
(31)

This scaling is an approximation, and its duration must match the intended rate coordinate. One can use fixed observation-based durations to avoid changing weights during optimization. If weights are recomputed from fitted prices, the objective itself changes with parameters and the implementation must account for that.

Quote uncertainty and robust losses

Weights based on bid–ask widths can reduce the influence of poorly measured quotes, but a near-zero spread should not imply infinite weight. Apply a defensible floor and examine whether spreads genuinely measure observation uncertainty. A robust loss can reduce sensitivity to isolated outliers; it does not eliminate the need to investigate stale quotes or incorrect schedules.

Fitting inside bid–ask bands rather than targeting every mid quote exactly is another approach. A model price within a band can incur little or no residual penalty, while a price outside it is penalized by distance to the band. This changes the identification problem: several parameter sets may be equally acceptable within market precision.

The dataset used here

The synthetic study starts from sixteen continuous zero observations. Thirteen enter an equal-weight zero-rate loss, and three are withheld. Small deterministic perturbations are added to the reference curve. The observations already use matched conventions; no coupon-bond inversion or bootstrap uncertainty is hidden in the inputs.

The figure compares Nelson–Siegel and Svensson on that dataset. A more flexible model reduces residual structure, but the difference in training fit should be assessed together with validation and conditioning. The browser's calibration audit reports both training and withheld RMSE in basis points.

17 / Numerical calibration

Variable projection and numerical identification

For fixed decay times, Nelson–Siegel and Svensson zero rates are linear in their rate coefficients. Exploit that structure instead of asking a generic optimizer to estimate every parameter simultaneously.

Conditional linear estimation

Let X(τ)X(\tau) contain the loading rows at observed maturities, β\beta the coefficient vector, yy observed zero rates and WW a positive diagonal weight matrix. The profiled problem is:

β*(τ)=argminβ‖W1/2[X(τ)β−y]‖2,Jprof(τ)=Jz(β*(τ),τ).\beta^*(\tau)=\arg\min_\beta \left\|W^{1/2}[X(\tau)\beta-y]\right\|^2,\qquad J_{\mathrm{prof}}(\tau)=J_z(\beta^*(\tau),\tau).
(32)

Search one nonlinear decay parameter for Nelson–Siegel or two for Svensson. At every candidate, solve the small linear least-squares problem. This is variable projection: the linear unknowns are eliminated conditionally, leaving a lower-dimensional nonlinear objective.

Use QR or singular-value decomposition rather than explicitly inverting XTWXX^{\mathsf T}WX. Normal equations square the design matrix's condition number and can lose precision when loading columns are similar. A rank threshold should detect cases where separate coefficients cannot be reliably identified.

Searching over positive scales

Parameterize τk=euk\tau_k=e^{u_k} and search in log time. This guarantees positivity and treats multiplicative changes naturally. A coarse bounded grid supplies starting regions; local refinement improves candidates. Several starting points reduce the risk of selecting an inferior local optimum.

Bounds are not innocuous. An optimum at a decay bound suggests that the data prefer a scale outside the admissible region or do not identify it strongly. Widening the bounds may reduce residuals while making coefficients or extrapolation unstable. Report the boundary behavior instead of quietly accepting it as a measured maturity scale.

What the browser actually computes

The laboratory performs linear least squares with modified Gram–Schmidt QR and a second orthogonalization pass. It searches a logarithmic grid, retains eight candidates and refines them by bounded pattern search. Nearly rank-deficient designs are rejected. Coefficients outside ±15% are rejected rather than solved by a fully constrained linear optimizer.

This is a practical educational search over an admissible candidate set. Rejection of an unconstrained coefficient solution is not equivalent to solving the bounded linear subproblem at that decay. Consequently the browser does not claim an exact constrained global minimum. Its numerical method and limits are stated in the audit panel.

The static study uses multistart SciPy least squares on the profiled decay objective, with SVD-based linear estimation. It provides an independently implemented comparison. Both methods use the same training observations; neither uses withheld observations to tune its coefficients.

Curve stability versus coefficient stability

A parameter vector can be unstable while the fitted curve remains stable over observed maturities. Nearly redundant columns allow large coefficient movements that cancel in XβX\beta. Conversely, stable-looking coefficients can still imply risky extrapolation if the data do not cover the relevant payment dates.

Inspect design conditioning, multiple-start solutions, objective profiles and the effect of small quote perturbations. Report economically relevant outputs such as bond prices and key-rate risk alongside parameter estimates. A six-decimal coefficient is not evidence that the corresponding economic factor is identified to six decimals.

Price fitting is less separable

The variable-projection simplification applies directly to zero-rate least squares. In price space, discounts contain exponentials of the coefficients, so bond prices are nonlinear even when decay times are fixed. A price-space optimizer can still use analytical Jacobians and sensible starts, but it cannot simply reuse the same linear solve and claim to minimize price residuals.

18 / Model assessment

Residual analysis, validation and uncertainty

A calibration residual is the difference between a model output and an observation in the chosen coordinate. A validation residual uses observations excluded from fitting. Both are valuable, but they answer different questions.

RMSEA=1|A|∑i∈A[z(Ti;p)−yi]2,RMSEbp=104RMSE.\mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathcal A} =\sqrt{\frac1{|\mathcal A|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal A} [z(T_i;p)-y_i]^2},\qquad \mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{bp}}=10^4\mathrm{RMSE}.
(33)

Patterns matter beyond one average

A low overall RMSE can conceal a persistent long-end error or an isolated maturity with a large discrepancy. Plot residuals against maturity, duration, liquidity and instrument type. A systematic hump in residuals may indicate missing model flexibility. A bond-specific outlier may indicate a quote or schedule problem rather than a term-structure feature.

Compare price residuals with bid–ask widths or reporting resolution where those are available. A tiny yield residual on a thirty-year bond can matter more financially than a larger short-bill yield residual. Validation should therefore include the portfolio's relevant price and risk coordinates.

Withheld maturities

The synthetic fit withholds 0.75, 4 and 15 years. Its training and validation sets are fixed before fitting. Nelson–Siegel gives training RMSE 2.321190 bp and withheld RMSE 2.755916 bp. Svensson gives 0.242440 bp and 0.598699 bp respectively in the static calculation. These numbers describe this deliberately constructed dataset, not a general ranking on real markets.
