7Training3.174788%3.175759%+0.097128
10Training3.141333%3.142134%+0.080107
12Training3.129700%3.129605%-0.009490
15Withheld3.125308%3.126040%+0.073194
20Training3.146454%3.144690%-0.176432
25Training3.173893%3.176010%+0.211731
30Training3.210186%3.209410%-0.077564

The Svensson fit has more flexibility and the generating curve itself belongs to that family. Its better validation result is therefore unsurprising. A broader comparison would test many dates, different noise patterns and curve regimes. One favourable synthetic example does not establish a universally preferred market model.

Cross-sectional and time-series validation

Withholding maturities assesses interpolation across the current cross-section. Withholding future dates assesses forecasting. These should not be confused. A curve can interpolate a date's instruments accurately while its factors are poor predictors of tomorrow's rates.

For time-series research, fit on the information available at each historical date. Do not use revised curves, future instrument eligibility or a decay selected using the complete future sample without acknowledging that information. A smooth parameter time series can be a result of hindsight choices rather than stable real-time estimation.

Parameter and output uncertainty

Locally, if the residual Jacobian JJ is well conditioned and the observation-error model is appropriate, an approximate coefficient covariance can be related to (JTWJ)−1(J^{\mathsf T}WJ)^{-1}. This approximation can fail near bounds, rank deficiency or multiple minima. It also omits model misspecification unless specifically extended.

A perturbation study often communicates uncertainty more directly: shift quotes within defensible error ranges, recalibrate and observe changes in discounts, forwards, bond values and hedges. Bootstrapping observations can be useful when its sampling assumptions fit the data, but maturity observations are not necessarily independent identically distributed draws.

Validation tolerances should reflect the application. A macroeconomic chart may tolerate several basis points of smoothing error; a hedging engine may require much tighter instrument repricing and stable sensitivities. State the acceptable error in the coordinates that matter to the task.

19 / Unobserved maturities

Boundary behavior and long-horizon extrapolation

Extrapolation begins where reliable observations end. A formula continuing smoothly beyond the last quote is still a modelling assumption. The issue is especially important when a liability's cash flows extend much further than the instruments used to estimate the curve.

Parametric asymptotes

Nelson–Siegel and Svensson converge to β0\beta_0 in zero and instantaneous forward rates. Their zero loadings decay partly at inverse maturity speed, so the asymptotic regime may be reached slowly. A thirty-year fitted zero need not equal the model's long-run level.

limT→∞z(T)=β0,limT→∞f(T)=β0.\lim_{T\to\infty}z(T)=\beta_0,\qquad \lim_{T\to\infty}f(T)=\beta_0.
(34)

When β0>0\beta_0>0, discounts tend to zero. When β0<0\beta_0<0, discounts grow at long horizons within the mathematical representation. A finite negative-rate model can be useful over observed maturities without making its infinite-horizon extrapolation economically suitable.

Alternative tail rules

A flat-zero tail sets z(T)=z(T*)z(T)=z(T_*) beyond the last maturity T*T_*. It makes the tail forward equal that fixed zero rate and can create a forward jump at the boundary. A flat-forward tail instead continues the integrated rate linearly:

h(T)=h(T*)+f*[T−T*],D(T)=D(T*)e−f*(T−T*).h(T)=h(T_*)+f_*[T-T_*],\qquad D(T)=D(T_*)e^{-f_*(T-T_*)}.
(35)

These tails generally differ. A gradual convergence to an assumed ultimate forward rate supplies another rule, but the ultimate rate and convergence speed then become explicit external assumptions. Such conventions can be useful for an application with prescribed valuation rules; they are not observations extracted from absent long-end quotes.

Boundary smoothness

Matching the discount level ensures price continuity at the splice. Matching the forward also ensures first-derivative continuity of the log discount. Matching higher derivatives can produce a smoother chart, but additional smoothness is not an economic requirement for every task. Choose boundary conditions for their consequences, rather than aesthetics alone.

The short end also requires assumptions. A curve fitted only to bonds beyond one year may estimate a short limit with substantial uncertainty. Policy-meeting jumps, known overnight fixings and settlement effects can make a smooth parametric extrapolation inappropriate for short-dated derivatives.

Price sensitivity to tail assumptions

A small long-end zero difference is multiplied by maturity in the discount exponent. For a zero-coupon payment at fifty years, a 20 bp continuous-zero difference changes its price ratio by e−50×0.002≈0.904837e^{-50\times0.002}\approx0.904837, about a 9.52% reduction. The rate discrepancy looks small, while its present-value effect can be material.

Compare several defensible tail specifications, identify cash flows beyond the observed region and report their contribution to total value. If the portfolio's main risk lies in extrapolated maturities, in-sample quote RMSE is a weak description of valuation reliability.

20 / Time evolution

Dynamic factors, affine models and HJM consistency

A cross-sectional curve can be fitted anew each day, producing a time series of level, slope and curvature factors. A dynamic model adds a transition law and a probability measure. Forecasting under the physical measure and derivative valuation under a pricing measure require different assumptions.

Dynamic Nelson–Siegel

With a fixed decay time, let btb_t collect time-varying Nelson–Siegel coefficients. A simple statistical specification is a vector autoregression:

zt(θ)=X(θ;τ)bt,bt+1=a+Abt+εt+1.z_t(\theta)=X(\theta;\tau)b_t,\qquad b_{t+1}=a+Ab_t+\varepsilon_{t+1}.
(36)

Here θ\theta is remaining maturity, not a fixed calendar payment date. One can estimate factor transitions and forecast future curve shapes under the physical measure. Fixing decay improves comparability of the factors across dates, but can limit fit when the curve's characteristic scale changes.

Diebold and Li develop forecasting with a dynamic factor interpretation of Nelson–Siegel. That statistical framework is useful for predictions; an additional restriction is needed to obtain a fully specified no-arbitrage pricing model. Forecasting the Term Structure of Government Bond Yields.

Affine short-rate models

An affine model represents bond prices through exponential-affine functions of state variables. A schematic form is:

Dt(T)=exp[A(T−t)−B(T−t)Txt].D_t(T)=\exp\left[A(T-t)-B(T-t)^{\mathsf T}x_t\right].
(37)

The functions A,BA,B are determined by the state dynamics and pricing assumptions, rather than chosen independently for each maturity. Mean-reverting Gaussian short-rate models permit negative rates; square-root models have different positivity properties under their admissible parameter conditions. Model choice affects option prices and transition behavior even when today's curve is matched.

Arbitrage-free Nelson–Siegel models reconcile Nelson–Siegel-like loadings with affine pricing restrictions and typically include a yield adjustment. Simply adding an arbitrary stochastic process to today's fitted coefficients is not the same construction. Christensen, Diebold and Rudebusch, The Affine Arbitrage-Free Class of Nelson–Siegel Term Structure Models.

Heath–Jarrow–Morton drift restriction

In a standard HJM setting under the money-market risk-neutral measure, with Brownian drivers Wℚ,kW^{\mathbb Q,k} and absolute maturity TT, instantaneous forwards satisfy:

df(t,T)=α(t,T)dt+∑k=1dσk(t,T)dWtℚ,k,α(t,T)=∑k=1dσk(t,T)∫tTσk(t,u)du.df(t,T)=\alpha(t,T)\,dt+\sum_{k=1}^{d}\sigma_k(t,T)\,dW_t^{\mathbb Q,k},\qquad \alpha(t,T)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\sigma_k(t,T)\int_t^T\sigma_k(t,u)\,du.
(38)

Under the required regularity and tradability assumptions, specifying forward volatility fixes its pricing-measure drift. Under the physical measure, market prices of risk alter the drift. This illustrates the distinction between matching one initial curve and specifying consistent stochastic evolution across all bond maturities. Heath, Jarrow and Morton, technical-report precursor.

Choosing a dynamic model for a task

For a forecasting exercise, assess out-of-time errors and economic interpretation. For an interest-rate option model, assess derivative calibration, volatility structure and pricing-measure consistency. For a stress test, deterministic scenarios may be sufficient without asserting probabilities. These are different uses of the same initial curve.

The laboratory on this page is a static construction and fixed-cash-flow valuation tool. Its synthetic factor figure illustrates time-varying shapes without claiming a fitted VAR, stochastic simulation or derivative model. The curve is the starting condition for those extensions, rather than their complete solution.

21 / Fixed-income risk

Duration and convexity under curve shifts

A rate sensitivity must identify the rate being moved. Shifting every continuously compounded zero by the same amount is a different experiment from shifting one bond's nominal YTM or one market swap quote.

Parallel continuous-zero shifts

Let zs(t)=z(t)+sz_s(t)=z(t)+s, so Ds(t)=D(t)e−stD_s(t)=D(t)e^{-st}. For nonnegative fixed cash flows:

P(s)=∑iCiD(ti)e−sti,P'(0)=−∑itiCiD(ti),P''(0)=∑iti2CiD(ti).P(s)=\sum_i C_iD(t_i)e^{-st_i},\qquad P'(0)=-\sum_i t_iC_iD(t_i),\qquad P''(0)=\sum_i t_i^2C_iD(t_i).
(39)
Dz=−P'(0)P=∑itiPViP,Cz=P''(0)P=∑iti2PViP.\mathcal D_z=-\frac{P'(0)}P=\frac{\sum_i t_iPV_i}{P},\qquad \mathcal C_z=\frac{P''(0)}P=\frac{\sum_i t_i^2PV_i}{P}.
(40)

Duration is the present-value-weighted average payment time, in years. Convexity is the corresponding second moment, in years squared. Both are positive for positive cash flows at positive future dates. A zero-coupon bond has duration TT and convexity T2T^2 under this continuous-zero shift.

Approximations and DV01

P(s)≈P[1−Dzs+12Czs2],DV01linear=10−4PDz.P(s)\approx P\left[1-\mathcal D_zs+\frac12\mathcal C_zs^2\right],\qquad \mathrm{DV01}_{\mathrm{linear}}=10^{-4}P\mathcal D_z.
(41)

This page reports DV01 as the positive first-order price loss for a +1 bp shift. The exact loss P(0)−P(0.0001)P(0)-P(0.0001) differs slightly because of convexity. Some systems report a signed derivative or a central-difference amount; identify the convention rather than assume every field called DV01 has the same sign.

For the reference five-year 4% semiannual bond, duration is 4.588041 years, convexity 22.201609 years² and linear DV01 0.047560 per face 100. A +100 bp shift gives exact price 99.017346, compared with 98.904138 from duration alone and 99.019209 from duration plus convexity.

Nominal-YTM duration

For a regular bond valued with nominal YTM yy compounded mm times per year, differentiation of (1+y/m)−mti(1+y/m)^{-mt_i} gives:

Dy=∑itiPVi(y)P(y)(1+y/m),Cy=∑iti(ti+1/m)PVi(y)P(y)(1+y/m)2.\mathcal D_y= \frac{\sum_i t_iPV_i(y)}{P(y)(1+y/m)},\qquad \mathcal C_y= \frac{\sum_i t_i(t_i+1/m)PV_i(y)}{P(y)(1+y/m)^2}.
(42)

The numerator's weighted time is often called Macaulay duration in that yield representation. Dividing by 1+y/m1+y/m gives modified duration. These quantities use the single-yield present values, which can differ from the individual curve-discounted present values even when total price agrees.

Why the distinction matters

A curve-based risk report should use derivatives matching its shock definition. Combining a continuous-zero parallel shock with a nominal-YTM modified duration introduces a convention error. Bumping market quotes and recalibrating introduces another layer of dependence: the resulting zero changes are usually not parallel.

The Taylor expansion is local. Large shifts, long maturities and instruments with negative or contingent cash flows can require exact repricing. Callable bonds and mortgage-like cash flows change with rates, so fixed-payment duration alone omits exercise or prepayment effects. The laboratory restricts itself to fixed cash flows and always shows an exact repricing alongside approximations.

A portfolio's signed cash-flow sums can have a small net price and large offsetting sensitivities. Normalized duration can then become misleading or unstable. Dollar sensitivities and scenario changes remain informative even when dividing by net value does not.

22 / Distributed curve risk

Key-rate sensitivities and calibration risk

Parallel duration compresses the curve's risk into one number. A portfolio can be insensitive to a parallel move yet highly sensitive to a steepening or a localized long-end change. Key-rate sensitivities distribute risk over maturity regions.

A defined bump basis

Choose functions wk(t)w_k(t) and perturb the zero curve by z(t)↦z(t)+skwk(t)z(t)\mapsto z(t)+s_kw_k(t). The sensitivity to a unit decimal bump is:

∂P∂sk=−∑itiPViwk(ti),KRDk=−1P∂P∂sk.\frac{\partial P}{\partial s_k} =-\sum_i t_iPV_iw_k(t_i),\qquad \mathrm{KRD}_k=-\frac1P\frac{\partial P}{\partial s_k}.
(43)

Triangular hat functions on a grid of maturities are one convenient choice. Each is one at its own node, zero at adjacent nodes and linear between. Different choices, including spline bumps or piecewise-constant forward bumps, generate different key-rate reports.

The parallel-risk identity

If the bump functions form a partition of unity over all payment dates, ∑kwk(t)=1\sum_kw_k(t)=1, their normalized sensitivities sum to parallel zero duration:

∑kKRDk=Dz.\sum_k\mathrm{KRD}_k=\mathcal D_z.
(44)

The endpoint functions are part of that partition. Omitting the shortest or longest hat can leave cash flows outside the covered risk basis. A failure of the sum test may therefore reveal an incomplete bump convention rather than a derivative error.

Parameter risk and quote risk

Nelson–Siegel factor sensitivities follow the corresponding loadings. Holding decay fixed, a bump to β0\beta_0 is parallel; a bump to β1\beta_1 uses A(T/τ)A(T/\tau); a bump to β2\beta_2 uses B(T/τ)B(T/\tau). These parameter risks are useful for model interpretation but are not necessarily exposures to directly tradable instruments.

A market hedge report usually bumps observable quotes and recalibrates. If the fitted parameters are p(q)p(q), the chain rule gives:

dPdqj=∂P∂p∂p∂qj.\frac{dP}{dq_j}=\frac{\partial P}{\partial p} \frac{\partial p}{\partial q_j}.
(45)

The second factor contains the calibration response. It depends on instrument selection, interpolation, weights, bounds and whether other curves are rebuilt. A small quote change can cause large parameter movements near weak identification while leaving some prices nearly unchanged.

Numerical bump methodology

Use a specified bump amount, central or one-sided difference, recalibration tolerance and unit convention. Check several sensible bump sizes when numerical noise or constraint activation matters. A central difference can cross an active constraint and approximate a response that is not smooth at the reference quote.

For a multicurve system, label the bumped curve and the dependencies rebuilt. A tenor-basis quote can affect projected coupons while an overnight quote affects discounting and potentially recalibrated projections. Freezing one component versus rebuilding the whole system answers different hedge questions.

Hedge interpretation

Matching key-rate DV01 can reduce first-order exposure to the selected bump basis. It does not eliminate convexity, basis, credit, liquidity or model risk. Hedge instruments also have their own curve and convention sensitivities. A clean maturity-bucket picture is useful only when the construction behind it is explicit.

Compare risk maps across interpolation methods and plausible calibrations. If a hedge changes dramatically when a nearly equivalent curve is fitted, that instability is a material result even when both curves have small pricing residuals.

23 / Holding-period valuation

Forward carry, roll-down and economic interpretation

Carry and roll-down describe how value can evolve as time passes under specified assumptions. They are not automatically predictions of investment returns. Separate contractual coupon income, financing, the shortening of remaining maturity and changes in the future curve.

Forward bond prices

For a zero-coupon bond paying one unit at TT, its time-zero forward price for delivery at h<Th<T is:

F0,hbond(T)=D(T)D(h).F_{0,h}^{\mathrm{bond}}(T)=\frac{D(T)}{D(h)}.
(46)

The ratio follows from financing a position to delivery in the simple single-curve setting. It is not the unconditional physical expected future bond price. Under the appropriate forward measure, a pricing expectation can reproduce this value; under the physical measure, risk premia and dynamics affect the expectation.

For a coupon bond, subtract the time-zero present value of coupons paid before delivery from its current dirty price, then divide by D(h)D(h), with delivery-date coupon treatment specified. Convert the resulting delivery dirty value to a clean quote using accrued interest at that date if needed.

Static-curve roll-down

Under an unchanged maturity-indexed zero curve, a zero with remaining maturity T−hT-h is valued at:

Phstatic(T)=e−(T−h)z0(T−h).P_h^{\mathrm{static}}(T)=e^{-(T-h)z_0(T-h)}.
(47)

This assumption reuses today's zero at the shorter remaining maturity. It differs from following today's forward-implied discount ratio. On a sloped curve, static roll-down changes the bond's applicable zero rate as it ages. On a flat deterministic curve, the static and forward assumptions coincide for the zero bond.

Decomposing holding-period return

A realized return over a holding period includes sale value, coupon receipts and any reinvestment, compared with the initial cost and financing. A useful scenario analysis can compare an unchanged curve with parallel, twist and credit-spread scenarios. Each result should state the assumed future curve and reinvestment treatment.

For a coupon bond, calling the entire return “roll-down” obscures coupon income and financing. A precise decomposition also needs a convention for separating the pure passage of time from the rate change implied by the shorter maturity. Different desk reports can use different decompositions while agreeing on total scenario value.

Term premia and expectations

A long zero rate reflects more than a simple average of future physical short-rate expectations. Risk compensation and convexity affect the relationship. The exact formula depends on the dynamic model and probability measure. Inferring an expected policy-rate path from forwards therefore requires an interpretation layer beyond curve construction.

Similarly, an upward-sloping curve does not guarantee that borrowing short and investing long will earn a positive risk-adjusted return. Future rate changes, funding costs, leverage, liquidity and exposure to tail scenarios can dominate the initial spread. The curve supplies prices for dates; it does not remove the uncertainty between them.

Practical reporting

Report the initial dirty value, projected cash receipts, future dirty and clean values, funding assumption and curve-evolution scenario. This makes a carry estimate reproducible and comparable. For a risk-neutral forward valuation, identify the numeraire and distinguish the pricing relation from a real-world forecast.

The figure uses a five-year zero bond to isolate the distinction. One path holds the maturity-indexed curve unchanged; the other uses today's implied forward bond price. Their difference is an assumption about evolution, rather than an arithmetic inconsistency.

24 / Shape risk

Curve scenarios and principal-component risk

A scenario is an explicit change to the curve. It can be motivated by history, a statistical model or a deterministic stress design. Define the shifted object and maturity function so the result can be reproduced.

Level, twist and belly shocks

A parallel continuous-zero shock adds a constant. A twist raises one end relative to another. A belly shock concentrates the move around intermediate maturities. On a thirty-year grid, illustrative functions are:

slevel(T)=0.01,stwist(T)=0.005(T15−1),sbelly(T)=0.005exp[−(T−74)2].s_{\mathrm{level}}(T)=0.01,\qquad s_{\mathrm{twist}}(T)=0.005\left(\frac{T}{15}-1\right),\qquad s_{\mathrm{belly}}(T)=0.005\exp\left[-\left(\frac{T-7}{4}\right)^2\right].
(48)

The twist runs from −50 bp at zero to +50 bp at thirty years. The belly peaks at +50 bp near seven years. These definitions are chosen educational scenarios, rather than empirical estimates. Applying them to zero rates implies corresponding forward shocks:

Δf(T)=s(T)+Ts'(T),Dscenario(T)=D(T)e−Ts(T).\Delta f(T)=s(T)+Ts'(T),\qquad D_{\mathrm{scenario}}(T)=D(T)e^{-Ts(T)}.
(49)

A smooth-looking zero twist can therefore create a larger long-end forward movement. Scenario labels should not substitute for checking the actual rate and discount transformations.

Principal-component analysis

Given historical changes in rates at a fixed maturity grid, estimate a covariance matrix and diagonalize it. If Σvk=λkvk\Sigma v_k=\lambda_kv_k, the eigenvectors define orthogonal directions under the selected grid and normalization. A one-standard-deviation scenario for component kk can be represented as λkvk\sqrt{\lambda_k}v_k.

Major components are often interpreted as level, slope and curvature when their shapes support those labels. They need not equal Nelson–Siegel loadings or the deterministic shocks above. Results depend on the sample window, change horizon, rate coordinate, maturity grid and whether the data are standardized.

Units and normalization

A covariance built from rates in percent differs numerically from one built from decimals. Multiplying all observations by 100 multiplies covariance by 10,000 and standard deviations by 100. Eigenvector signs are arbitrary, so a historical “positive slope factor” requires a reporting orientation convention.

Using a correlation matrix standardizes maturity variances and emphasizes a different risk metric from covariance PCA. Adding densely spaced long-end maturities also changes the implicit weighting. Document those choices before interpreting explained variance as an intrinsic property of the market.

Portfolio application

Reprice the portfolio under each shape scenario, or project a sensitivity vector onto the scenario direction for a first-order approximation. Exact repricing matters when shifts are large or when options change cash flows. A portfolio hedged against the first component can retain significant second- or third-component exposure.

Historical PCA is descriptive and sample dependent. It does not establish Gaussian tails, stationarity or that future stress follows the same eigenvectors. Complement it with explicit policy, liquidity, basis and long-end scenarios where those risks matter.

The laboratory focuses on parallel zero shocks because their duration and convexity have transparent formulas. The static scenario figure extends the geometry to shape moves, while the key-rate framework provides the natural bridge to a fuller interactive scenario engine.

25 / Implementation practice

Reproducible construction and research workflow

A curve should be reproducible from a dated input snapshot, conventions and algorithm settings. A saved parameter vector alone cannot explain which instruments were selected, how their cash flows were generated or why particular residuals were accepted.

Separate the layers

Keep market observations, contract schedules, pricing equations, curve representation, optimization and reporting as distinct components. This separation allows a schedule correction to be tested without rewriting the optimizer, and an interpolation experiment to be compared using identical instruments.

  1. Capture observations. Store source, timestamp, bid/ask or price, instrument identifier, settlement convention and eligibility decision.
  2. Generate schedules. Preserve adjusted and unadjusted dates, accrual fractions, payment amounts and principal.
  3. Choose the curve architecture. Identify discount and forecast roles, interpolation coordinate and tail rules.
  4. Calibrate. Record objective, weights, parameter domains, starting points, convergence criteria and fit diagnostics.
  5. Validate and report. Reprice instruments, check coordinate identities, evaluate relevant risk and export results with units.

Minimum numerical checks

Test D(0)=1D(0)=1, positivity of discounts, stable zero-time limits and recovery of rate conversions. Compare analytical forwards with derivatives of integrated rates. Verify an annual par bootstrap against independently generated discounts. Compare bond duration and convexity with finite differences under the matching curve shift.

For a synthetic exact model, calibration should recover prices or rates within the intended tolerance, but parameter recovery may be nonunique when columns are redundant. Judge output recovery separately from parameter recovery. A test that demands identical coefficients in a rank-deficient case asserts information that the data do not contain.

Audit optimization

Record unsuccessful starts as well as the best candidate, at least in the research audit. Repeat selected fits after small data perturbations and examine boundary solutions. Use a second numerical implementation for core formulas where an error would materially alter the interpretation.

Version input data and conventions. A daily curve can change because market prices changed, the instrument universe changed, a calendar was corrected or the algorithm changed. Those causes have different implications for a factor time series. An undocumented construction revision can resemble an economic shock.

Reporting units and exports

A CSV column named zero_continuous_decimal is more informative than rate. Include maturity years, discount factors, curve family and parameter values. If a quote is stored in basis points, put that in its field name. Avoid exporting rounded displayed strings as computational inputs.

The downloadable laboratory curve contains sampled continuous zeros, instantaneous forwards, base discounts and shocked discounts, together with model parameters and shock amount. The separate on-page cash-flow ledger supports the selected bond valuation. The export is a synthetic model result, not a market-data file.

Performance and model selection

Cache schedules and loading matrices where inputs permit. A low-dimensional parametric fit should be fast enough to inspect several starts and diagnostics; speed is not a reason to remove those checks. More complicated joint multicurve construction benefits from sparse dependencies and analytic Jacobians.

Choose complexity for the task. Broad curve interpretation may favour a parsimonious family; precise pricing may require local construction; derivative valuation requires dynamics and volatility calibration. Reusing one curve representation across these tasks is possible, but its adequacy must be established in each role.

26 / Numerical laboratory

Interactive term-structure and bond laboratory

The laboratory computes a continuous Nelson–Siegel or Svensson curve, its analytical instantaneous forwards, discounts, semiannual par rates and a selected fixed-coupon bond. Every output is calculated locally. The static notes and plots remain readable without JavaScript.

Reading the rate and price panels

The first plot compares continuous zero and instantaneous forward rates with a continuous-equivalent semiannual par coupon. The second panel shows base and shifted discounts. The separate sensitivity plot compares exact bond prices under parallel continuous-zero shifts with first- and second-order approximations.

Hover over a plot to inspect every represented curve at the same horizontal coordinate. The compact neutral inspector follows the pointer, flips near viewport edges and highlights the nearest line. Touch pins an inspection; a tap outside dismisses it. Keyboard arrows move through samples, up and down switch panels, and Escape dismisses the inspector. Values between samples describe the displayed line interpolation.

Suggested experiments

  1. Raise the level coefficient by 0.5 percentage points. Observe the parallel zero shift, discount reduction and bond price change.
  2. Change a decay time while keeping rate coefficients fixed. Compare the movement of the zero hump with the forward hump.
  3. Select Nelson–Siegel and fit the synthetic quotes, then repeat with Svensson. Compare training and withheld RMSE, not just the fitted chart.
  4. Set a negative short-rate limit through the slope coefficient. Inspect discounts above one and read the stated negative-rate assumption.
  5. Increase bond maturity and apply a +100 bp shift. Compare exact repricing with duration and convexity, keeping their shock convention fixed.

Calibration controls and scope

“Fit synthetic quotes” uses only thirteen training maturities. The three withheld quotes remain visible for assessment. The audit describes the browser search and reports both errors. “Build curve” compares manually selected parameters with the same dataset. “Reset reference” restores the generating parameter set, rather than the fitted noisy-data parameters.

Bond coupons are nonnegative, schedules use exact-year intervals and valuation occurs on a coupon date. The selected bond frequency controls its cash flows and nominal YTM. The plotted par curve always uses semiannual coupons, independently of the selected bond. A zero coupon is supported by setting the coupon rate to zero.

4.52.0000000.8664657481.732931
5102.0000000.85249528286.954519
Total103.660106

The total is 103.660106. Since the coupon exceeds the relevant par coupon, price is above 100. Solving the nominal semiannual YTM equation gives 3.201986%. The terminal zero is 3.191752% continuous, while the five-year semiannual par coupon is 3.204782%. These numbers should not be equated without both structural and compounding distinctions.

Approximately 83.88% of present value comes from the final combined coupon and principal. Earlier coupons reduce weighted payment time below maturity, giving continuous-zero duration 4.588041 rather than five. Convexity is 22.201609 rather than the zero-coupon value of 25.

Study C: a +100 bp parallel zero shock

Shift every continuous zero by 0.01, so each discount is multiplied by e−0.01te^{-0.01t}. The selected coupon and principal amounts remain fixed. This produces the following comparison:

Parallel continuous-zero shift of +0.01 · amounts per face 100
MethodBond priceApproximation minus exact
Base103.660106—
Exact +100 bp99.0173460.000000
Duration98.904138-0.113208
Duration + convexity99.019209+0.001863

The quadratic approximation misses exact price by about 0.001863 per face 100. Duration alone understates the shocked price because positive convexity bends price upward relative to its tangent. Both are local approximations, and neither changes the bond's contractual payments.

Study D: fitting noisy synthetic zero observations

At the sixteen specified maturities, generate observations using the following rule, indexing ii from zero:

yi=zref(Ti)+0.00012sin(7i)+0.00004cos(3i).y_i=z_{\mathrm{ref}}(T_i)+0.00012\sin(7i)+0.00004\cos(3i).
(50)

Withhold indices whose remainder modulo five is two. Thus 0.75, 4 and 15 years are not used in either fit.

The fitted Svensson decay times are approximately 1.462960 and 7.706554 years, rather than the generating 1.6 and 6.5. The fitting procedure targets the perturbed quotes, so exact recovery of generating parameters is not the objective. The withheld error remains below one basis point in this example.

Nelson–Siegel cannot reproduce the same second-curvature feature as closely. Its fitted long level is approximately 3.153683%, compared with Svensson's 3.510110%. Both can look plausible over observed maturities while implying different far-horizon limits. This connects fit flexibility directly to extrapolation and long-liability valuation.

Study E: negative short rates

Select Nelson–Siegel coefficients β0=0.005\beta_0=0.005, β1=−0.020\beta_1=-0.020, β2=0.008\beta_2=0.008, with τ=2\tau=2. The short-rate limit is −1.5%, while the long limit is 0.5%. Discounts initially rise above one and eventually decline as positive accumulated rates dominate. The representation remains positive everywhere; its economic use requires a framework allowing negative rates.

The purpose of this example is to test the distinction between discount positivity and discount monotonicity. A diagnostic should identify negative forwards and the relevant assumption, rather than automatically replace them with zero and silently alter the fitted curve.

28 / Mathematical appendix

Mathematical appendix and reference implementation

Integrating the Nelson–Siegel forward basis

For x=T/τx=T/\tau, the first exponential term integrates to τ(1−e−x)\tau(1-e^{-x}). The curvature-forward term integrates to τ[1−(1+x)e−x]\tau[1-(1+x)e^{-x}]. Dividing by TT gives the zero loadings:

1T∫0Te−u/τdu=A(x),1T∫0Tuτe−u/τdu=1−(1+x)e−xx=B(x).\frac1T\int_0^T e^{-u/\tau}\,du=A(x),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\frac{u}{\tau}e^{-u/\tau}\,du =\frac{1-(1+x)e^{-x}}x=B(x).
(51)

The second curvature term in Svensson integrates identically at its own time scale. This derivation verifies the analytical forward formula; forwards should not be fitted separately in a way that breaks the integration identity.

Small-argument expansions

A(x)=1−x2+x26−x324+x4120+O(x5),B(x)=x2−x23+x38−x430+O(x5).A(x)=1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{6}-\frac{x^3}{24} +\frac{x^4}{120}+O(x^5),\qquad B(x)=\frac{x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{3}+\frac{x^3}{8} -\frac{x^4}{30}+O(x^5).
(52)

Use these expansions near zero and an exponential-minus-one function elsewhere. The origin then evaluates to the analytical short limit. Switching thresholds can be checked by comparing both expressions near the switch, rather than assuming a threshold supplies continuity automatically.

Loading derivatives

A'(x)=(x+1)e−x−1x2,B'(x)=A'(x)+e−x.A'(x)=\frac{(x+1)e^{-x}-1}{x^2},\qquad B'(x)=A'(x)+e^{-x}.
(53)

The zero curvature maximum solves ex=x2+x+1e^x=x^2+x+1, excluding the zero boundary, giving x≈1.793282x\approx1.793282. The forward curvature derivative is e−x(1−x)e^{-x}(1-x), so its maximum is at one. These loading maxima do not generally locate the maximum of the full zero or forward curve.

Parameter derivatives and price Jacobians

For fixed decay times, ∂z/∂βk\partial z/\partial\beta_k is the corresponding loading. Since x=T/τx=T/\tau, ∂x/∂τ=−T/τ2\partial x/\partial\tau=-T/\tau^2. For the first Svensson decay:

∂z∂τ1=−Tτ12[β1A'(x1)+β2B'(x1)],∂z∂τ2=−Tτ22β3B'(x2).\frac{\partial z}{\partial\tau_1} =-\frac{T}{\tau_1^2} \left[\beta_1A'(x_1)+\beta_2B'(x_1)\right],\qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial\tau_2} =-\frac{T}{\tau_2^2}\beta_3B'(x_2).
(54)
∂P∂pk=−∑itiCiD(ti)∂z(ti)∂pk.\frac{\partial P}{\partial p_k} =-\sum_i t_iC_iD(t_i)\frac{\partial z(t_i)}{\partial p_k}.
(55)

These derivatives support efficient price-space calibration and parameter-risk reports. Near the origin, use series for the loading derivatives as well to avoid cancellation. A numerical check should perturb each parameter in its own units, especially when mixing rate coefficients and decay times.

A compact Python reference

The implementation below reproduces the curve and the reference bond. It uses decimals and exact-year schedules. It is intentionally separate from the browser implementation, providing a simple formula reference rather than a full market-calendar library.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import brentq

def basis(T, tau):
    x = np.asarray(T, dtype=float) / tau
    small = np.abs(x) < 1e-5
    safe = np.where(small, 1.0, x)
    A = -np.expm1(-x) / safe
    A = np.where(small, 1-x/2+x*x/6-x**3/24+x**4/120, A)
    return A, A - np.exp(-x)

def nss(T, p):
    b0, b1, b2, b3, tau1, tau2 = p
    T = np.asarray(T, dtype=float)
    A1, B1 = basis(T, tau1)
    _, B2 = basis(T, tau2)
    x1, x2 = T/tau1, T/tau2
    z = b0 + b1*A1 + b2*B1 + b3*B2
    f = (b0 + b1*np.exp(-x1) + b2*x1*np.exp(-x1)
         + b3*x2*np.exp(-x2))
    return z, f, np.exp(-T*z)

p = [0.035, -0.020, 0.025, -0.015, 1.6, 6.5]
t = np.arange(1, 11) / 2
cf = np.full(10, 2.0)
cf[-1] += 100.0
pv = cf * nss(t, p)[2]
price = pv.sum()
duration = (t*pv).sum() / price
convexity = (t*t*pv).sum() / price
ytm = brentq(
    lambda y: np.sum(cf/(1+y/2)**np.arange(1, 11)) - price,
    -1.8, 2.0
)
print(price, ytm, duration, convexity)
# 103.66010585  0.03201986  4.58804082  22.20160889

Conditional least-squares reference

At a candidate pair of decay times, form columns 1,A(T/τ1),B(T/τ1),B(T/τ2)1,A(T/\tau_1),B(T/\tau_1),B(T/\tau_2) and call numpy.linalg.lstsq. The residual is the design prediction minus observed zeros. Search over positive decay times using multiple starts, and assess rank and conditioning before interpreting coefficients.

If bounds on coefficients are essential, solve a bounded linear subproblem at each decay candidate rather than rejecting an unconstrained solution and declaring the result an exact constrained optimum. The browser's rejection method is clearly labelled; a production implementation can replace it with a suitable constrained solver.

29 / Exercises

Exercises and worked solutions

Work in decimals unless a question requests a displayed percentage. Specify the rate and payment convention before calculating. Solutions are expandable and can also be included when printing the notes.

Exercise 1 — Recover a zero rate from a price

A default-free zero pays 100 in ten years and costs 85. Find its discount factor, continuous zero and effective annual yield.

Solution. The discount is 0.85. The continuous zero is −ln(0.85)/10≈0.016251893-\ln(0.85)/10\approx0.016251893, or 1.625189%. The effective annual yield is e0.016251893−1≈1.638467%e^{0.016251893}-1\approx1.638467\%. Both reproduce price 85; using the same numerical rate under both conventions would not.

Exercise 2 — Convert nominal compounding

A nominal semiannual zero rate is 4%. What is the continuous equivalent and the five-year discount?

Solution. z=2ln(1.02)≈0.039605255z=2\ln(1.02)\approx0.039605255, or 3.960525%. The discount is 1.02−10≈0.8203483001.02^{-10}\approx0.820348300. Applying 4% continuous compounding would give e−0.2≈0.818730753e^{-0.2}\approx0.818730753, which is a different price.

Exercise 3 — Compute a simple forward

Discounts at 0.5 and one year are 0.99 and 0.97. With an accrual fraction of 0.5, find the simple forward and continuous interval forward.

Solution. The simple forward is (0.99/0.97−1)/0.5≈4.123711%(0.99/0.97-1)/0.5\approx4.123711\%. The continuous forward is 2ln(0.99/0.97)≈4.081774%2\ln(0.99/0.97)\approx4.081774\%. Their equivalent accumulation factors over the interval agree.

Exercise 4 — Derive a two-year par coupon

Annual coupon dates have discounts 0.98 and 0.95. What annual coupon rate makes a two-year bond worth 100?

Solution. c=1−0.950.98+0.95=0.025906736c=\frac{1-0.95}{0.98+0.95}=0.025906736, or 2.590674%. Coupons are 2.590674 per face 100. Their present value plus discounted principal is 100. The terminal continuous zero is −ln(0.95)/2-\ln(0.95)/2, a different quantity.

Exercise 5 — Bootstrap an annual par node

The one-year annual par quote is 2% and the two-year annual par quote is 2.5%. Express the recovered one- and two-year discounts.

Solution. D(1)=1/1.02D(1)=1/1.02. Then D(2)=[1−0.025D(1)]/1.025D(2)=[1-0.025D(1)]/1.025. Reinsert both discounts into 1=0.025[D(1)+D(2)]+D(2)1=0.025[D(1)+D(2)]+D(2). The second quotation identifies the terminal discount only after the earlier coupon discount has been supplied.

Exercise 6 — Interpret Nelson–Siegel endpoints

Let level be 3%, slope −1% and curvature 2%, with any positive finite decay time. What are the short and long limits?

Solution. Both zero and forward short limits are 3%−1%=2%3\%-1\%=2\%. Both long limits are 3%. The curvature factor vanishes at the endpoints, so changing it affects intermediate maturities while preserving these limits. The shape in between also depends on decay time.

Exercise 7 — Recover the marginal forward

At five years, the zero is 3% and its slope is 0.001 per additional year. Find the instantaneous forward.

Solution. f=z+Tz'=0.03+5(0.001)=0.035f=z+Tz'=0.03+5(0.001)=0.035, or 3.5%. The derivative's units are rate per year. The forward exceeds the zero because the marginal addition to integrated rates is above the prior average.

Exercise 8 — Identify a log-linear forward segment

Continuous zeros are 2% at two years and 3% at three years. Interpolate log discounts between those dates. What is the instantaneous forward inside the segment?

Solution. Integrated rates are 0.04 and 0.09. Their linear slope is (0.09−0.04)/(3−2)=0.05(0.09-0.04)/(3-2)=0.05, so the segment forward is 5%. Interpolating the zeros themselves would produce a different forward function despite matching the same endpoints.

Exercise 9 — Diagnose redundant Svensson factors

Why is a Svensson fit with equal decay times unable to identify both curvature coefficients separately?

Solution. The two curvature loading columns coincide. Replacing β2\beta_2 by β2+a\beta_2+a and β3\beta_3 by β3−a\beta_3-a leaves the curve unchanged. Only their sum is identified. A rank-aware solver should detect the redundancy rather than report two uniquely estimated factors.

Exercise 10 — Price and risk of a zero bond

A seven-year zero is worth 80. Under a parallel continuous-zero shift, find duration, convexity and linear DV01.

Solution. Duration is seven years and convexity is 49 years². Linear DV01 is 80×7×0.0001=0.05680\times7\times0.0001=0.056. Exact +1 bp loss is 80[1−e−0.0007]80[1-e^{-0.0007}], slightly below 0.056 because of positive convexity.

Exercise 11 — Apply duration and convexity

A bond costs 105, has continuous-zero duration seven and convexity 55. Estimate price after a +50 bp parallel shift.

Solution. Set s=0.005s=0.005. The approximation is 105[1−7s+55s2/2]=101.3971875105[1-7s+55s^2/2]=101.3971875. Duration alone gives 101.325. The convexity correction is positive. The inputs must be derivatives of the same shift used in the scenario.

Exercise 12 — Audit key-rate coverage

Four reported key-rate durations sum to 5.8 years, while parallel duration is 6.1. Give two possible explanations.

Solution. The bump functions may not form a partition of unity over all cash flows, for example because endpoint hats are missing. Alternatively, the report may mix parameter or market-quote recalibration risks with direct zero-curve bumps. Compare definitions before assuming the difference is a numerical error.

Exercise 13 — Separate fitting from validation

A model has 0.2 bp training RMSE and 4 bp withheld RMSE. Does the training fit establish a reliable curve? What should be investigated?

Solution. No. Inspect maturity-specific residuals, observation noise, parameter conditioning, sparse regions and model flexibility. Check whether withheld data were inadvertently used in model selection. A small training residual can arise from overfitting, while the desired outputs may be especially sensitive in the poorly validated region.

Exercise 14 — Interpret an implied policy path

A forward curve rises from 2% to 4%. Explain why this is insufficient to conclude that the market's physical expected short rate follows exactly that path.

Solution. Forward rates are pricing coordinates. Their expectation interpretation depends on the probability measure, risk premia, payoff and curve family. Sovereign credit or liquidity effects may also enter. The curve can supply a precise discount ratio without uniquely identifying a real-world policy forecast.

30 / References

References and further reading

Primary research and institutional methodology underpin the model definitions and context. The explanations, synthetic dataset, numerical studies, figures and offline implementation on this page are developed for these notes. Source conventions should be checked before using institutional curve data.

  1. Nelson, C. R. and Siegel, A. F. (1987). Parsimonious Modeling of Yield Curves. Journal of Business, 60(4), 473–489. Published paper; 1985 NBER working-paper precursor.

    The three-factor exponential-loading representation and parsimonious estimation.

  2. Svensson, L. E. O. (1994). Estimating and Interpreting Forward Interest Rates: Sweden 1992–1994. NBER Working Paper 4871. Author working paper.

    The second curvature factor and interpretation of implied forward curves.

  3. Bank for International Settlements (2005). Zero-Coupon Yield Curves: Technical Documentation. BIS Papers No. 25. Technical documentation.

    A comparison of central-bank curve-construction approaches and conventions.

  4. Gürkaynak, R. S., Sack, B. and Wright, J. H. (2006). The U.S. Treasury Yield Curve: 1961 to the Present. FEDS 2006-28. Federal Reserve research paper.

    Smooth Treasury-curve estimation, instrument selection and empirical construction.

  5. Hagan, P. S. and West, G. (2006). Interpolation Methods for Curve Construction. Applied Mathematical Finance, 13(2), 89–129. Research paper.

    Interpolation properties, forward behavior and their interaction with bootstrapping.

  6. Diebold, F. X. and Li, C. (2003). Forecasting the Term Structure of Government Bond Yields. NBER Working Paper 10048. Working paper; published in Journal of Econometrics, 130(2), 337–364 (2006).

    Time-varying Nelson–Siegel factors and term-structure forecasting.

  7. Christensen, J. H. E., Diebold, F. X. and Rudebusch, G. D. (2010 revision). The Affine Arbitrage-Free Class of Nelson–Siegel Term Structure Models. Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Working Paper 2007-20. Author working paper.

    Affine no-arbitrage restrictions and Nelson–Siegel-like term structures.

  8. Heath, D., Jarrow, R. and Morton, A. (1992). Bond Pricing and the Term Structure of Interest Rates: A New Methodology for Contingent Claims Valuation. Econometrica, 60(1), 77–105. Published paper; Cornell technical-report precursor.

    The connection between forward volatility and pricing-measure drift.

  9. Bianchetti, M. (2009; revised 2010). Two Curves, One Price: Pricing & Hedging Interest Rate Derivatives Decoupling Forwarding and Discounting Yield Curves. Author preprint.

    Distinct discount and forecasting roles, tenor basis and multicurve valuation.

  10. European Central Bank. Euro Area Yield Curves: General Description of Methodology. Official methodology.

    Definitions, instrument universe and the Svensson approach for published government curves.

  11. Bank of England. Yield Curves. Official data and methodology.

    Published curve families, continuous compounding, forward interpretation and practical conventions.

A reading path

Start with the discount, compounding and forward identities, then reproduce the bootstrap and reference bond. Read Nelson–Siegel and Svensson alongside the calibration audit. Study interpolation before evaluating market hedges, and move to dynamic factor or HJM research only after distinguishing cross-sectional fit from time evolution.

For further implementation, extend the payment engine with real schedules and calibrate to quoted instrument prices. For a research project, compare model stability across dates and withheld maturities. For interest-rate options, add a dynamic pricing framework and volatility calibration rather than assuming the initial yield curve determines option values.
